wolves.label: disputed

quote: Popular stories suggest it was once the refuge of wolves (lycos in Greek), which is possibly the origin of its name
Another etymology suggests a Pelasgian, pre-Mycenean, origin

quote: Mythologically, Lycabettus is credited to Athena, who created it when she dropped a limestone mountain she had been carrying from the Pallene peninsula for the construction of the Acropolis

paras.t: Lycabettus is the highest point in central Athens, 277 metres above sea level. You can ride the funicular from Aristippou Street in Kolonaki, or walk the paved path, which Wikivoyage reckons takes about 30 minutes.
If you walk, you'll climb through pines that cover the lower slopes of this big limestone hill.

parts.name: At the top
parts.stand: On the terrace beside the small white chapel, looking southwest toward the Acropolis.

paras.t: Here's your reward. Take a moment to look out over the city and find the Acropolis.
Up here are the little Chapel of Saint George, from the 1800s, a restaurant, and just below, an open-air theatre that reopened in September 2023 after 15 years closed.

And the name? It may come from the Greek word for wolf, from a time when wolves roamed here, or from an older, pre-Greek word. Nobody's sure. There's a myth too: Athena was carrying a mountain to build up the Acropolis, dropped it, and here it is.
Stay for sunset if you can, and then watch the city lights come on.

practical.t: Funicular times and fares change; check before you go.
